text: Problem §1 Introduction, §2 Related work By 2018, pretraining a language representation on unlabelled text and then transferring it was clearly effective: ELMo, ULMFiT and OpenAI GPT had all improved many tasks with it ( §1 , §2 ).
label: core

text: There were two ways to transfer.
label: core
key: There were two ways to transfer.

text: The feature-based way (ELMo) feeds pretrained representations as extra features into a task-specific architecture.
label: core

text: The fine-tuning way (GPT) adds a few task parameters and fine-tunes all the pretrained ones.
label: core

text: Both pretrained with the same kind of objective: a unidirectional language model ( §1 ).
label: core

text: That is the handicap the paper attacks.
label: core
key: That is the handicap the paper

text: A standard language model can only be trained left to right (or right to left), because in a deep network that conditions on both sides each word could indirectly "see itself" through the higher layers ( §3.1 ).
label: core

text: So GPT's Transformer lets every token attend only to tokens on its left, and ELMo's two directions are separate, shallow LSTMs whose outputs are merely concatenated ( §2.1 , Figure 3 ).
label: core

text: For sentence-level tasks this is sub-optimal; for token-level tasks such as question answering and named entity recognition, where the context on the right of a word is essential, it "could be very harmful" ( §1 ).
label: core

text: The gap: a way to pretrain a genuinely deep bidirectional model on unlabelled text that transfers to many tasks, sentence-level and token-level, with minimal task-specific architecture.
label: core
key: The gap: a way to pretrain

text: Pretraining task 1: the masked LM §3.1, Appendix A.1 The data generator picks 15% of the WordPiece positions of each sequence at random.
label: core

text: Their final states T i go through a softmax over the vocabulary and are trained with cross-entropy to predict the original token; unlike a denoising autoencoder, nothing else is reconstructed ( §3.1 ).
label: core

text: Masking is applied after WordPiece tokenisation, uniformly, with no special treatment of word pieces ( A.2 ); the authors later released Whole Word Masking models, which mask all the pieces of a word at once, because predicting one piece of a split word was "too 'easy'" ( repository README, 31 May 2019 ).
label: core

text: A [MASK] token never appears at fine-tuning time, which creates a mismatch.
label: core

text: So a chosen position is not always masked ( §3.1 , A.1 ): Of the chosen 15% Example (the 4th token, hairy , chosen) Share of all tokens 80%: replaced by [MASK] my dog is hairy → my dog is [MASK] 12% 10%: replaced by a random word my dog is hairy → my dog is apple 1.5% 10%: left unchanged my dog is hairy → my dog is hairy 1.5% Because the encoder does not know which words it will be asked to predict, or which were swapped, it is forced to keep "a distributional contextual representation of every input token"; keeping some words unchanged biases the representation towards the observed word, and random replacement touches only 1.5% of tokens (10% of 15%), too few to harm understanding ( A.1 ).
label: core

text: The price: only 15% of positions produce a loss in each batch, against every position for a left-to-right model, so MLM should need more steps.
label: core

text: It does converge marginally slower, but its downstream accuracy overtakes the left-to-right model's almost immediately ( C.1 , Figure 5 below).
label: core

text: Pretraining setup §3.1 Pre-training data, Appendix A.2 Data: BooksCorpus (800M words) and English Wikipedia (2,500M words, text passages only, no lists, tables or headers).
label: core

text: A document-level corpus, not shuffled sentences like the Billion Word Benchmark, is "critical" to extract long contiguous sequences ( §3.1 ).
label: core

text: Examples: two spans sampled from the corpus, A and B, combined length at most 512 tokens, 50% IsNext ( A.2 ).
label: core

text: Batch and steps: 256 sequences of 512 tokens ("128,000 tokens/batch"; exactly 256 × 512 = 131,072 ) for 1,000,000 steps, "approximately 40 epochs over the 3.3 billion word corpus" (by the paper's own arithmetic 10 6 × 128,000 / 3.3 × 10 9 = 38.8 ).
label: core

text: Sequence length: attention is quadratic in length, so 90% of the steps use length 128 and the last 10% length 512, "to learn the positional embeddings".
label: core

text: Derived, with an assumption the paper does not state: if the batch stays 256 sequences at length 128, the run sees 0.9 × 10 6 × 256 × 128 + 0.1 × 10 6 × 256 × 512 ≈ 42.6 billion token positions, about 13 passes over 3.3 billion words rather than 40 (and WordPiece tokens outnumber words).
label: depth

text: Optimiser: Adam, learning rate 10 −4 , β 1 = 0.9, β 2 = 0.999, L2 weight decay 0.01, warmup over the first 10,000 steps then linear decay; dropout 0.1 on all layers; GELU ( Hendrycks and Gimpel 2016 ) instead of ReLU, following GPT.
label: core

text: Hardware: BERT-Base on 4 Cloud TPUs in Pod configuration (16 TPU chips), BERT-Large on 16 Cloud TPUs (64 chips); each took 4 days ( A.2 ).
label: core

text: BERT was deliberately built as close to GPT as possible so the two could be compared, but four other things differ ( A.4 ): BERT also trains on Wikipedia (GPT: BooksCorpus only); BERT learns [SEP] , [CLS] and the segment embeddings in pretraining (GPT adds them at fine-tuning); BERT's batch is 128,000 words against GPT's 32,000, both for 1M steps; and BERT picks a fine-tuning learning rate per task where GPT used 5e-5 for all.

text: Why it matters (beyond the paper) BERT ended the era of task-specific NLP architectures: after it the default recipe became "pretrain a big Transformer, fine-tune per task", and masked prediction became the canonical self-supervised objective for encoders.
label: core

text: A family of descendants followed: RoBERTa (the same model "significantly undertrained"; trained longer on 160GB, without NSP, with dynamic masking), ALBERT , ELECTRA , DistilBERT , DeBERTa and the multilingual XLM-R .
label: owned:models_and_training/topic_llm_architecture/families_and_objectives

text: The idea leaked beyond text: masked-prediction pretraining underpins vision methods such as BEiT and MAE , and pooled [CLS] -style representations underpin embedding models ( Sentence-BERT ).
label: owned:models_and_training/topic_ml_fundamentals/contrastive_and_self_supervised_learning

text: It also cemented the GLUE and SQuAD leaderboard culture, and Table 6 was an early clean demonstration that scaling model size keeps paying even on small downstream sets.
label: core

text: Decoders won generation, but encoder-only models never went away where one cheap forward pass must produce a representation rather than text: BERT descendants dominate embedding and retrieval stacks (bi-encoders for vector search such as DPR , cross-encoder rerankers such as monoBERT , late interaction in ColBERT ), plus classification, moderation and NER at production scale.
